Title: Reply to every 1-2 star review within 24 hours, with a route to a fix
Owner: Customer support lead, with one engineer on call for app issues
Problem: Unhappy reviewers are almost never answered. Most developer replies go to people who were already happy.
Evidence: 29 of 769 low-star reviews got a reply (3.8%); median reply time 58.3 hours; 62.0% of replies went to 4-5 star reviews.
Suspected cause: Replying looks ad hoc and unowned. MoveInSync's own blog credits personal, non-canned replies for an earlier recovery (4.3 back to 4.6), so this is a practice that lapsed, not one that needs inventing.
Change: Name one owner for the Play review inbox and set a 24-hour target for 1-2 star reviews. | Use the weekly reply queue this project generates (unanswered low-star reviews, each with a drafted reply and its theme). | Each reply does three things: names the specific problem, gives one concrete next step (a fix version, or app@moveinsync.com with what to include), and asks the reviewer to update the review once it is sorted. | For reviews with no detail ("worst app"), ask what went wrong. That is a quarter of all low-star reviews we currently learn nothing from.
First step: Tomorrow, work through the newest 20 unanswered low-star reviews in the reply queue.
Already exists?: Replies exist today but are rare and slow; figures below are from the public reply data on each review.
Success metric: Share of 1-2 star reviews replied to within 24 hours, from under 5% to over 90%.
How to verify: The monitor reports reply rate and reply time weekly. Track how many replied-to reviewers later raise their rating (Play Console shows edited ratings).
Guardrail: No canned text. Never offer anything in exchange for a rating change; Google prohibits incentivised ratings.

Title: Remove the false "not downloaded from Play Store" block on Android
Problem: Users who installed from the Play Store are told the app "was not downloaded from Play Store" and locked out until they reinstall, often every few days. "App won't open" is the fastest-growing complaint.
Evidence: 54 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (7.0%); 31.5% on iOS. 9 low-star Play reviews mention the "not downloaded / installed from Play Store" message (7 in the last 90 days). 7 low-star Play reviews name a specific phone or Android version that cannot open the app (6 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: Suspected: an installer-source or Play Integrity check that treats a failed or timed-out check as tampering. The complaints begin in July 2026 around version 12.16, which suggests when it was introduced or tightened. Separate crash reports name Android 17, OnePlus 12 and Pixel devices.
Change: Make the integrity check fail open. When it cannot get an answer, let the user in and log the event instead of blocking. | Retry in the background, and only block on a definite "tampered" verdict. | Add the check's pass, fail and error rates to release monitoring. | Reproduce the Android 17 and OnePlus 12 crashes from Play Console crash clusters.
First step: Search the Android codebase for the user-facing string, find the check behind it, and pull its failure rate by app version.
Already exists?: Not documented in the help center. Reviewers quote the message nearly word for word, so the string should be easy to find.
Success metric: Low-star reviews quoting this message fall to zero in the first full month after release.
How to verify: The monitor counts this phrase weekly. Confirm with the crash-free and ANR rates in Play Console vitals.
Guardrail: If the check exists for a security requirement, keep the logging and server-side verdict; only the lock-out on error goes.

Title: Stop putting prompts between the employee and their ride
Owner: Product manager for the employee app, with Android and iOS engineering
Problem: Employees open the app in a hurry to find a cab number or an OTP, and the app makes them do something else first: rate the previous trip with no skip, accept the transport policy again, dismiss a banner, or answer a microphone permission request. Some came to the Play Store to give one star specifically because of the forced rating.
Evidence: 40 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (5.2%); 5.5% on iOS. 12 low-star Play reviews object to a forced or repeated trip rating (4 in the last 90 days). 8 low-star Play reviews object to accepting the transport policy or "I agree" repeatedly (1 in the last 90 days). 25 low-star Play reviews object to notifications, pop-ups or banners (6 in the last 90 days). 6 low-star Play reviews object to repeated permission requests (3 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: Each prompt was probably added for a good local reason (feedback volume, compliance, campaigns). Nobody owns the total. Trip feedback is a configurable setting in the admin dashboard, so some of this may be set per customer.
Change: Trip rating gets a visible Skip, and never blocks the current trip card. | Transport policy is accepted once per policy version, not on every open. | A permission that has been declined is not requested again on launch; ask only at the moment the feature is used. | Full-screen banners are removed from app open; the trip card is always the first thing shown. | Set one rule for the app - nothing may appear before the current trip - and review every new prompt against it.
First step: List every screen that can appear between app open and the current trip card, with who owns each. Ship Skip on trip rating first.
Already exists?: The help center shows trip feedback is switchable per site (Ticket Management Config > Trip Feedback). Check whether "mandatory" is a product default or a customer choice before changing it.
Success metric: Median time from app open to the trip card. Low-star reviews in this theme fall by half within two releases.
How to verify: Theme share in the weekly monitor, plus in-app analytics on prompt views and skips.
Guardrail: Trip-feedback volume will fall when it becomes optional. Agree that with Ops before shipping; feedback given under compulsion is poor data anyway.

Title: Triage every safety-flagged review within 24 hours
Owner: Head of safety or operations, with customer support
Problem: A small number of reviews describe real risk to a person: abusive or speeding drivers, women left without a cab or a door drop at night, an SOS button or helpdesk that could not be reached. These are few, so a ranking by volume buries them.
Evidence: 25 safety-flagged low-star reviews in 12 months (Play and iOS).
Suspected cause: Play reviews are not treated as an incident channel, so a safety report made there waits with everything else.
Change: The monitor already flags these separately. Route that list to a named safety owner each week, and same-day for new ones. | Reply publicly within 24 hours asking for trip details through a private channel, and open an incident. | Check the specific product claims - SOS not working, pop-ups blocking SOS, forced logout blocking SOS - as P1 bugs.
First step: Read the safety queue in this report today and open incidents for any that name a place, vehicle or date.
Already exists?: The app has SOS and a helpdesk; reviewers report cases where neither could be reached. We could not test them.
Success metric: Every safety-flagged review has a reply and an incident reference within 24 hours.
How to verify: Weekly count of safety-flagged reviews without a reply, target zero.
Guardrail: Never ask for personal or trip details in the public reply.

Title: Fix login OTP delivery, and tell the user why no OTP came
Owner: Backend / identity engineering, with customer onboarding
Problem: The largest single named complaint is that the login OTP never arrives by SMS, email or WhatsApp, so the employee cannot book or track anything. It is also the second-largest complaint on iOS, so it is not an Android bug. It has run at a steady rate for two years.
Evidence: 92 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (12.0%); 12.7% on iOS. 61 low-star Play reviews mention OTP (12 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: Two different problems probably share one symptom. First, delivery failures at the SMS or email provider. Second, the employee is not registered: the help center says OTP depends on the number or email in the employer's records and on profile permissions, and a reviewer points out the app gives no message saying whether the number is registered. An unregistered user just waits for an OTP that will never be sent.
Change: Measure the funnel by channel and by customer: OTP requested, sent, delivered, entered, verified. | When the number or email is not in the employer's records, say so on screen, with who to contact, instead of failing silently. | Fall back automatically to a second channel after a timeout, and show which channel was used. | Keep sessions alive across network drops; a forced logout puts the user back through OTP at the worst moment.
First step: Pull one week of OTP logs and split failures into "never sent (not registered)" and "sent but not delivered". The split decides who fixes it.
Already exists?: The help center has a troubleshooting article for OTP not received, so the problem is known. Repeated-logout complaints have nearly stopped since late 2025, which suggests an earlier fix there worked.
Success metric: OTP verification success rate, and low-star reviews in this theme.
How to verify: Theme share in the weekly monitor on Play and iOS.
Guardrail: The "not registered" message must not reveal whether a given number belongs to a customer to someone probing; show it only after a rate-limited attempt.

Title: Gate every release on crash rate and early reviews
Problem: The app ships every one to two weeks, and reviewers repeatedly report that an update broke something for them: the app no longer opens on their phone, crashes on the tracking screen, or stopped supporting their iOS version. On iOS, "won't open" is by far the largest complaint.
Evidence: 85 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (11.1%); 37.6% on iOS. 13 low-star iOS reviews (iOS) describe a crash while tracking or on the map (0 in the last 90 days). 12 low-star iOS reviews (iOS) name an older iPhone or iOS version that stopped working (1 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: Suspected: releases go to all users at once, and the test device list does not cover the newest Android version or older iPhones still in use. Dropping iOS 15 and 16 appears to have happened without warning to users.
Change: Use Play staged rollouts: 5%, then 20%, then 100%, with an automatic halt if the crash-free rate or the share of 1-star reviews on the new version crosses a set line. | Add to the pre-release device list: the newest Android version, the top five devices by user count, and the oldest supported iPhone. | Before dropping an OS version, show an in-app notice for two releases. | Write release notes that say what changed, so support and customers can connect a complaint to a version. Nearly every recent note says only "bug fixes".
First step: Turn on staged rollout for the next release and set the halt thresholds from the last three months of Play Console vitals.
Already exists?: No version in the last year is provably worse than the baseline on review data alone, because per-version samples are small. Crash and ANR rates in Play Console will show it properly, and we do not have those.
Success metric: Crash-free users per release, and the share of low-star reviews that blame an update.
How to verify: The monitor's per-version table and "after update" flag.
Guardrail: A halted rollout needs a named person who decides to resume or roll back.

Title: Ask for a Play rating at the right moment, starting where the listing is weakest
Owner: Product manager for the employee app
Problem: Most riders are satisfied and never rate; people with a problem do. The rating also differs by country, and the listings outside India are lower and rest on far fewer ratings, so a small number of new ratings moves them. Meanwhile at least two reviewers say the app already asks for Play reviews after every ride, and one lowered a 5-star rating to 3 because of it.
Evidence: listing ratings: United States 4.32, Philippines 4.49, United Kingdom 4.49, South Africa 4.62, India 4.64, Sri Lanka 4.65, Singapore 4.65. 2 Play reviews of any rating complain about being asked to review the app (1 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: The review request appears to be triggered by frequency, not by a good experience, which annoys regular riders and wastes Google's quota for showing the dialog.
Change: Use the Play In-App Review API, triggered only by objective success - for example the third consecutive on-time completed trip with no complaint raised. | Cap it at once per user per quarter. Google limits how often the dialog shows anyway. | Prioritise countries where the listing is lowest (see the table), since those averages move fastest. | Do not ask "are you enjoying the app?" first, and do not send only happy users to the store.
First step: Find out what triggers the current review request and how often it fires per user.
Already exists?: Two reviewers also say an in-app rating screen accepted only high stars. We could not verify this. If it is a pre-screen for the Play prompt, remove it.
Success metric: Rating shown on each country listing, and number of new ratings per week.
How to verify: The monitor records every country listing weekly and, from the second run, the star mix of newly added ratings.
Guardrail: Google's guidance: trigger "after a user has experienced enough of your app", "don't prompt the user excessively", and do not "ask the user any questions before or while presenting the rating button or card, including questions about their opinion". The trigger must be an event, never a sentiment check.

Title: Give employees a complaint route that works, so the Play Store stops being one
Owner: Product manager for support tooling, with the operations lead
Problem: About one in five specific complaints is about the service, not the app: late or missing cabs, long routes, driver conduct. MoveInSync cannot fix a vendor's lateness from the app. But many of these reviewers say they tried to complain first and could not: the helpdesk was busy or cut the call, a bug report errored, there was no way to give feedback on a trip.
Evidence: 123 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (16.0%); 13.3% on iOS. 31 low-star Play reviews mention the helpdesk, helpline or customer support (9 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: When the in-app route fails, the public review becomes the complaint form, and the app takes the one star for a vendor's failure.
Change: One button on every trip card: Report a problem with this trip. Pre-filled with the trip, a short list of reasons, optional text. | Each report gets a visible status and a reply, and goes to the customer's transport desk and to the vendor. | Fix the reported failures in the existing channels - the feedback text box, the bug-report submission, helpdesk calls dropping. | Give each customer a monthly view of complaints by vendor, so lateness is managed where it is caused.
First step: Test every existing complaint path in the app end to end and list which ones fail. Reviewers name at least three.
Already exists?: Trip feedback and a ticketing configuration exist in the admin dashboard. Whether a ticket reaches the employee with a status, we could not see.
Success metric: Share of trip problems reported in-app with a response within 24 hours. Service-owned low-star reviews fall.
How to verify: Owner split in the weekly monitor (app, operations, policy).
Guardrail: Do not route unhappy users away from the Play Store rating prompt; this is a complaint channel, not a filter on who gets asked to rate.

Title: Make tracking and trip details trustworthy
Problem: Employees plan their morning around the pickup time and the cab's position, and both are often wrong: a location that is an hour stale, an ETA that jumps from 5 minutes to 30, a pickup time that changes overnight, a cab number or co-passenger list that is missing. People miss cabs because of it, and then get marked as no-shows.
Evidence: 90 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (11.7%); 4.8% on iOS. 46 low-star Play reviews mention calling the driver (10 in the last 90 days). 5 low-star Play reviews want to see co-passengers or their pickup points (2 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: Suspected: the position comes from the driver's phone and goes stale without the app saying so; the ETA does not account for stops before the rider; trip details are fetched live each time with no cached copy.
Change: Show how old the vehicle position is ("updated 4 min ago") and say so plainly when the driver's phone is offline. | Compute ETA from remaining stops and traffic, and show a range when it is uncertain. | Stop the map from resetting the user's zoom. | Notify when the pickup time changes by more than five minutes. | Keep the last trip card (cab number, driver, OTP) available offline; basements and parking levels have no signal. | Make "call driver" reliable, or say clearly when the employer has disabled it.
First step: Measure ETA error (shown ETA against actual arrival) per customer for one week. It sizes the problem and sets the target.
Already exists?: The help center says the boarding OTP appears once the driver accepts the trip. An offline copy is not described.
Success metric: Median ETA error, and low-star reviews in these two themes.
How to verify: Theme share in the weekly monitor.
Guardrail: Some missing details are employer choices (calling disabled by policy). Show the reason instead of a blank.

Title: Make no-shows fair and unsurprising
Problem: Being marked a no-show carries a penalty with some employers (warnings, lost booking rights, salary deductions), and reviewers describe it happening when the cab was late, when the driver never called, or after they missed a check-in without realising. The volume is low, the anger is high.
Evidence: 13 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (1.7%); 0.0% on iOS. 21 low-star Play reviews mention a no-show (6 in the last 90 days).
Suspected cause: The help center confirms that at trip end the system marks anyone not signed in as a no-show automatically, and that a driver can mark one too. Nothing warns the employee beforehand.
Change: Remind the employee to check in when the vehicle reaches their pickup point; a reviewer asked for exactly this. | Before a driver can mark a no-show, require a logged call attempt through the app and a minimum wait at the pickup point. | Never auto-mark a no-show on a trip where the cab arrived late. | Let the employee dispute a no-show from the trip history, with the GPS trace attached. | Clear old no-show notices from the home screen.
First step: Pull last month's no-shows and count how many were on late trips or had no call attempt. That is the size of the unfair share.
Already exists?: The help center describes a no-show cut-off and a policy-enforcement mode with warnings and schedule removal. A pre-warning or dispute flow is not described.
Success metric: Disputed no-shows as a share of all no-shows, and low-star reviews mentioning no-show.
How to verify: The monitor counts no-show mentions weekly.
Guardrail: Penalties are the employer's policy. Change the evidence and the warning, not the customer's rule.

Title: Close the booking and address traps
Problem: Booking mistakes cost a commute: a trip cancelled by an accidental tap with no confirmation, a date that defaults to the wrong day, a shuttle booking that became two steps so people thought they had booked when they had not, an address that cannot be changed or maps to the wrong spot. Separately, employees blame the app for rules their employer set, such as booking cut-offs and how far ahead they can book.
Evidence: 67 of 769 low-star Play reviews in 12 months (8.7%); 8.5% on iOS.
Suspected cause: Redesigns shipped without a way back or a warning, and employer rules are enforced without explanation.
Change: Confirm before cancelling a trip, especially from a notification. | After any booking, show a clear booked state, and an unmissable "not booked yet" state when a step remains. | Show the date being booked in words ("Mon 14 Oct") and never change it silently. | Let employees request an address or pickup-point change in the app, with status. | When a rule blocks a booking, say whose rule it is and what it is ("Your employer allows bookings up to 12 hours before the shift").
First step: Watch five employees book a shuttle and cancel a trip on the current version; note every hesitation.
Already exists?: Cut-offs and nodal points are configured per customer. The April 2026 release notes mention "improved booking flows", close to when redesign complaints begin.
Success metric: Booking completion rate, accidental-cancellation rate (cancel then rebook within 10 minutes), and low-star reviews in these themes.
How to verify: Theme share in the weekly monitor.
Guardrail: Roll booking-flow changes out in stages (see R6) with a way for customers to preview them.
